# LevitateOS

> LevitateOS is a Linux distribution where you maintain your own packages. Packages are Rhai scripts called "recipes" that declare how to acquire, build and install each piece of software, and every recipe runs inside an isolated Ginux domain. The installed system updates atomically: A/B slots are the default, each update is trial-booted before it is kept, and mutable mode is an explicit opt-in.

LevitateOS targets power users who want full control over their system. It follows the Arch Linux philosophy of a manual, step-by-step installation from a live ISO, but takes its core system pre-built from signed packages and replaces the traditional package manager with recipes.

Variants (built by the same pipeline):
- **LevitateOS**: glibc, systemd, GNU. Core system from signed Fedora 45 RPMs. Maximum compatibility.
- **AcornOS**: musl, OpenRC, busybox. Core system from Alpine Linux APKs. A smaller, simpler base.

Hardware baseline: x86-64-v3 (Intel Haswell or AMD Zen or newer), 16 GB RAM, NVMe disk, UEFI with Secure Boot disabled. First releases are planned for 2027, x86_64 first.

---

## Core Concepts

### What is a Recipe?

A recipe is a `.rhai` script that declares a package's facts and how to acquire, build and install it. Rhai is a small scripting language embedded in Rust. Every recipe runs inside an isolated Ginux domain (https://github.com/gmkurtzer/ginux): it sees only the inputs it is given at `/inputs/NAME`, reaches only the network hosts it is granted, and never runs on the host system. Downloads require a SHA-256 and git checkouts a full commit.

### Recipe Structure

Every recipe declares `const RECIPE_API = 2;`, a context map (`ctx`) and paired check/phase hooks. Checks return `ready(ctx)` or `needs_work(ctx, "reason")`; phase hooks return the updated `ctx`. Products are named in `ctx.outputs`.

```rhai
const RECIPE_API = 2;

let ctx = #{
    name: "ripgrep",
    version: "14.1.1",
    url: "https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/archive/14.1.1.tar.gz",
    sha256: "<pinned sha256>",
    src: join_path(RUNTIME.paths.build, "ripgrep-14.1.1"),
    bin: join_path(RUNTIME.paths.output, "usr/bin/rg"),
};

fn is_acquired(ctx) {
    if !is_file(join_path(ctx.src, "Cargo.toml")) {
        return needs_work(ctx, "source not unpacked");
    }
    ready(ctx)
}

fn acquire(ctx) {
    let dest = join_path(ctx.runtime.paths.build, "ripgrep.tar.gz");
    extract(download(ctx.url, dest, ctx.sha256), ctx.runtime.paths.build);
    ctx
}

fn is_built(ctx) {
    if !is_file(join_path(ctx.src, "target/release/rg")) {
        return needs_work(ctx, "rg not built");
    }
    ready(ctx)
}

fn build(ctx) {
    shell_in(ctx.src, "cargo build --release --locked");
    ctx
}

fn is_installed(ctx) {
    if !is_file(ctx.bin) { return needs_work(ctx, "rg not installed"); }
    ctx.outputs.rg = ctx.bin;
    ready(ctx)
}

fn install(ctx) {
    mkdir(dirname(ctx.bin));
    copy_file(join_path(ctx.src, "target/release/rg"), ctx.bin);
    chmod(ctx.bin, 0o755);
    ctx.outputs.rg = ctx.bin;
    ctx
}
```

### Lifecycle Phases

1. **Acquire**: fetch pinned sources (checksummed downloads, exact git commits)
2. **Build**: compile in `/work/build`
3. **Install**: place the product under `/out` and name it in `ctx.outputs`

Each phase has an `is_*` check that inspects the real files. Only `ctx.state` and its filesystem checkpoint are kept between runs, so an interrupted build resumes where it stopped.

### Runtime Paths

- `/inputs/NAME`: explicitly imported, read-only inputs
- `/work/build` (`runtime.paths.build`): owned build work
- `/work/tools` (`runtime.paths.tools`): shared dependency products
- `/out` (`runtime.paths.output`, `runtime.paths.target`): the product / target tree

---

## Atomic Updates

The disk holds two system slots (A and B) and a `/var` state partition. `recab` writes the next system into the inactive slot, carries the machine's configuration across (hostname, users, enabled services, network connections), and boots it once as a trial. A healthy trial is committed and becomes the default; a failed one falls back to the previous slot. `recab rollback` returns to the previous slot later. Recipe changes compose the inactive slot, never the running system. Mutable mode (one root, changed in place) is an explicit, unsafe opt-in.

```bash
recab stage --rootfs next.erofs --kernel vmlinuz --initrd initramfs.img
recab set-next B      # one trial boot of the staged slot
reboot                # committed if healthy, else back to A
recab rollback        # later, while A still holds its system
```

---

## Installation Process

The live ISO boots into the install screen: a guided app for each step, with a shell and the full guide beside it. The same steps by hand:

```bash
recpart apply --disk /dev/nvme0n1 --confirm DESTROY   # A/B layout, mounted at /mnt (--mode mutable for one root)
recstrap /mnt                                          # extract the system
recfstab /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab
recsetup inspect --root /mnt --json                    # choose target configuration
recsetup apply --root /mnt --hostname myhostname        # time zone, locale, accounts, boot, services
recchroot /mnt -- passwd                               # set the root password
```

### System Requirements

- CPU: x86-64-v3 (Intel Haswell or AMD Zen or newer)
- RAM: 16 GB
- Storage: NVMe disk
- Boot: UEFI, Secure Boot disabled (boot files are unsigned)

---

## Package Manager Commands

```bash
recipe install <recipe>       # acquire, build and install, publishing ctx.outputs
recipe remove <recipe>        # remove the product from the owned target
recipe cleanup <recipe>       # clean up build artifacts
recipe isinstalled <recipe>   # run is_installed(ctx)
recipe isbuilt <recipe>       # run is_built(ctx)
recipe isacquired <recipe>    # run is_acquired(ctx)
recipe list                   # list recipes in the recipes directory
recipe info <recipe>          # show declared recipe metadata
```

Common options: `--input NAME=PATH`, `--build-dir`, `--state-dir`, `--define KEY=VALUE`, `--json-output`, `--no-persist-state`.

- [Architecture FAQ](/docs/faq): Design decisions

### rec* Tooling

- [rec* Tooling Overview](/docs/rec-tooling-overview): Every rec* tool and what it does
- [Installation Tools Overview](/docs/installation-tools-overview): The tools used during installation
- [recpart](/docs/recpart): Partition planning and apply (like a scripted fdisk)
- [recstrap](/docs/recstrap): Extract the system image to a target directory (like pacstrap)
- [recfstab](/docs/recfstab): Generate fstab from mounted filesystems (like genfstab)
- [recsetup](/docs/recsetup): Configure an extracted system: time zone, locale, accounts, boot, services
- [recchroot](/docs/recchroot): Enter a chroot with the right bind mounts (like arch-chroot)
- [recab](/docs/recab): A/B slot manager: stage, trial boot, commit, rollback
- [recinit](/docs/recinit): Rootless initramfs builder
- [recuki](/docs/recuki): Unified Kernel Image builder
- [reciso](/docs/reciso): Bootable UEFI ISO builder
- [recqemu](/docs/recqemu): Runs test VMs as libvirt domains
